name: Actual run: eight voice AI interviews
request: Do the eight interviews support the three hypotheses H1 to H3 about voice AI customer support?

picks.name: Hypothesis tree
picks.reason: Splits each of H1 to H3 into sub-claims so every part of each hypothesis has something specific to look for in the eight interviews.

picks.name: Framework analysis
picks.reason: Builds an interview by hypothesis matrix so the pattern of support across all eight interviews is visible with an audit trail.

picks.name: Content analysis
picks.reason: Codes and counts how many interviews support, oppose or do not mention each hypothesis, giving an associational strength of statement.

picks.name: Reflexive thematic analysis
picks.reason: Reads the whole set for themes that emerge independently of H1 to H3, giving a different method to cross check the matrix and surface unexpected patterns.

picks.name: Comparative case study
picks.reason: Treats each interview as a case examined with the same questions, showing consistent patterns and deviant interviews.

picks.name: Analysis of competing hypotheses
picks.reason: Rates each evidence item against each hypothesis to show which evidence actually discriminates and which contradicts, serving the contradiction request.

picks.name: Disconfirmation search
picks.reason: Searches the interviews specifically for statements that would refute each hypothesis, so contradictions are found and not only confirmations.

picks.name: Stance detection
picks.reason: Labels each interview as favouring, opposing or neutral toward each hypothesis as an independent coding, so agreement with the human matrix adds confidence.

picks.name: Source-span and quotation check by code
picks.reason: Confirms each quoted passage cited as support or contradiction actually exists in the interview text, which matters for a decision-informing finding.

picks.name: Sensitivity analysis
picks.reason: Re-runs the support judgement under different coding and inclusion rules, such as dropping one interview, to see whether any conclusion reverses.

gaps: With eight interviews from one source these techniques support an associational statement only and cannot show how common a view is in the wider population or that voice AI causes any outcome. Interviewee selection, interviewer prompting and the unknown data condition are not tested, and the hypothesis wording is not checked for ambiguity.

# Comparative case matrix: eight interviews against H1 to H3

## Cases, questions and selection

Each participant is one case. The three questions put to every case are taken directly from the hypotheses:

- H1: Does the participant report the voice AI as more satisfying than traditional voice automation (or similar earlier automation)?
- H2: Does the participant say they would hang up on learning it is an AI?
- H3: Does the participant say they would immediately ask for a human agent?

Selection reason: the material gives no reason why these eight were chosen or why only some were quoted. It says only that each participant heard the same four prerecorded scenarios. The cases are therefore treated as comparable on exposure, but the basis of selection and of quote selection is unknown. P8 and P9 have no quotes, so their rows are empty and are not counted as support or as contradiction.

## Case by case matrix

| Case | H1: more satisfying than earlier automation? | H2: would hang up on learning it is an AI? | H3: would ask for a human straight away? |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Supports in Q1 ("this one seems to be pretty dynamic", compared with earlier chat bots that "never work"). Mixed in Q6 ("a little bit annoyed" because of previous experiences with AI agents). | No evidence. | Unclear. Q6 mentions that a human could be requested "at the beginning", but P1 does not say they asked for one. |
| P2 | Supports in Q2 ("It seemed like talking to a real person"), set against robot voices. | No evidence. | No evidence. |
| P3 | Supports in Q3 ("really excellent", "really seamless", no need to repeat yourself). | No evidence. | No evidence. |
| P4 | Mixed in Q5: initial reluctance, then "a really good process". No comparison with earlier automation is stated. | No evidence. | Against H3 in Q5 and Q9. Q5 says P4 would want "to speak to someone" at first, and Q9 puts asking at the introduction as where "I would do it". Both are conditional and hypothetical, and Q5 says the view changes as the process goes on. |
| P5 | Against in Q7 for the motor claim case: "extremely frustrated", voice "very cold in clinical". No comparison with earlier automation is stated. | Conditional in Q10: "I probably would've hung up" if no human was provided. | Against H3 in Q10: "I would've asked for a human." |
| P8 | No quotes in the material. | No quotes in the material. | No quotes in the material. |
| P9 | No quotes in the material. | No quotes in the material. | No quotes in the material. |
| P10 | Not a satisfaction comparison. Q4 objects to an "AI voice" that is "American" and wants a "local experience". | Against H2 in Q8: "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro." The stated reason is that the intro was "way too long". | No evidence. |

## Consistent patterns

1. H1 has support from three cases and no direct counter from any case that compared the AI with earlier automation. P1 (Q1), P2 (Q2) and P3 (Q3) describe the AI as more dynamic, more human or more seamless. The only explicit comparison with earlier automation is in Q1, and it refers to chat bots, not voice automation. Q2 and Q3 compare implicitly, with "robot voice" and with having to "repeat yourself". So the link in this sample is between human-like, responsive interaction and a favourable view, but the material does not contain a direct comparison with traditional voice automation.
2. Where participants express reservations, the stated reasons differ by case but each is about the specific context or delivery, not about the AI being unable to do the task. These are the stressful setting (P5, Q7), an accent and AI-sounding voice (P10, Q4), an overlong introduction (P10, Q8) and past experience with AI agents (P1, Q6).
3. Every statement against H2 or H3 is a stated intention ("would"), not a described event. No quote reports that a participant actually hung up or actually asked for a human.

## Deviant cases

- P10 deviates on H2. Q8 is the only unconditional statement of hanging up, and it is tied to the length of the introduction.
- P5 deviates on H1, H2 and H3 together, but only for the motor claim scenario in Q7, and the hang-up in Q10 is conditional on not getting a human.
- P4 deviates on H3 (Q9), though Q5 shows the initial reluctance fading.
- P1 is internally mixed, supporting H1 in Q1 and expressing annoyance in Q6, so P1 does not sit cleanly on either side.

## What this means for the three hypotheses

- H1: partly supported within this sample, by P1, P2 and P3, and opposed by P5 and, less directly, P10. Four of the eight participants (P1, P2, P3, P5) give a clear position on satisfaction. The comparison with traditional voice automation is not tested directly in any quote.
- H2: not supported by P10 (Q8), and P5 (Q10) hedges it. No other participant speaks to hanging up. The material cannot show that most participants would stay on the line.
- H3: not supported by P5 (Q10) and in part by P4 (Q5, Q9). No other participant speaks to it, and P1's Q6 is ambiguous.

For a decision, the usable finding is a split: some participants praise the voice AI, while the participants who object (P4, P5, P10) all say they would ask for a human or hang up. The material shows no case supporting H2 or H3 by an explicit statement, only the absence of statements from the other cases.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumes the cases are comparable and that the same questions can be asked of each. Here the quotes were not elicited with a common question, so each cell is filled from whatever the participant happened to say. Most cells are "no evidence", which is not the same as "no".
- The technique requires a stated reason for selecting each case. The material gives none, and the quotes are described as a subset. If quotes were chosen to show striking reactions, the matrix over-represents strong views.
- P8 and P9 could not be assessed. Six of eight cases have any evidence, and for H2 and H3 only P4, P5 and P10 do.
- Scenarios differ across quotes. Only Q7 names a scenario (motor claim). Differences between participants may reflect different scenarios or different stages of the call.
- No counts beyond what the quote IDs show are possible, and nothing here generalises beyond this sample.

## Alternative explanations

- The split on H1 may reflect scenario and stress, not individual differences. The sceptical quote Q7 is explicitly about a car accident, whereas the favourable quotes (Q1 to Q3) do not name a scenario. The same participants might respond differently to a sales call.
- The H2 and H3 deviations may reflect first impressions of the introduction (Q8, Q9) more than a general rejection of AI. P4 (Q5) says the view changes as the process goes on, so hang-up and human-request intentions may be tied to the opening only.
- Prior experience may explain the pattern. P1 refers to earlier chat bots and AI agents (Q1, Q6), so P1's comparison may be shaped by non-voice systems, which would weaken the link to H1 as written.
- Hypothetical statements ("would") from people listening to prerecorded scenarios may not match behaviour in a real call, so the deviant cases may overstate or understate real hang-up and human-request behaviour.

# Hypothesis tree: do the interviews support H1 to H3?

## Tree

Each node is a claim that must be true for its parent to be true. Evidence status is given for each leaf, using only Q1 to Q10 and participants P1 to P5 and P10. Statements are patterns within this sample only.

**R. The eight interviews support H1, H2 and H3.**
Reading: the root fails as stated. H1 has a favourable direction but cannot be tested as a comparison. H2 is neither supported nor refuted. H3 is contradicted by two quoted participants.

- **R1. H1: customers find voice AI interactions more satisfying than traditional voice automation.**
  - **R1.1 Participants express satisfaction with the voice AI scenarios.**
    - **R1.1a More quoted participants are favourable than unfavourable.**
      Status: mixed, leaning favourable. Favourable at least once: P1 (Q1, "this one seems to be pretty dynamic"), P2 (Q2, "it knew exactly what it needed to ask"), P3 (Q3, "really seamless") and P4 (Q5, "a really good process", reached only after initial reluctance). Unfavourable at least once: P1 (Q6, "I felt a little bit annoyed"), P5 (Q7, "I would be extremely frustrated"; Q7 is about a car accident scenario) and P10 (Q4, "it's American"; Q8, "it was way too long"). That is four participants against three, with P1 on both sides.
  - **R1.2 Participants judged the AI against earlier automated systems.**
    - **R1.2a Participants contrast the AI with earlier automation.**
      Status: supported for three participants. P1 (Q1, "those never work"), P2 (Q2, "sometimes when you are talking to a more of a robot, it sounds more like a robot voice") and P3 (Q3, "you have to repeat yourself").
    - **R1.2b The earlier automation they name is voice automation.**
      Status: partly supported. Only P2 (Q2) clearly refers to a voice. P1 (Q1) refers to chat bots that "parsed, um, articles from their own website", which is not voice automation. P3 (Q3) does not say what the earlier system was.
  - **R1.3 Satisfaction with voice AI and with traditional voice automation was assessed on the same basis for the same participants.**
    Status: no evidence possible (see list below).

- **R2. H2: customers do not hang up immediately when they learn they are speaking with an AI.**
  - **R2.1 Participants learn they are speaking with an AI at an identifiable point.**
    Status: no evidence possible. Q4 shows P10 recognising "an AI voice", but the material does not say whether the scenarios disclosed the AI or at what point.
  - **R2.2 Participants do not say they would end the call straight away.**
    Status: mixed. Against: P10 (Q8, "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro."). Conditional only: P5 (Q10, "I probably would've hung up and then tried to do it manually online", said after not getting a human). No such statement from P1, P2, P3 or P4, but silence is not evidence that they would stay. P4 (Q5) says the process becomes good as it goes on.
  - **R2.3 Any hang-up statement is caused by learning it is an AI, not by something else.**
    Status: unresolved. In Q8 P10 gives the length of the introduction as the reason ("it was way too long"). The same participant objects to the AI voice and its American accent in Q4. The material does not link either objection to the hang-up.
  - **R2.4 Stated intentions to hang up or stay reflect what participants would do in a live call.**
    Status: no evidence possible (see list below).

- **R3. H3: customers do not immediately ask for a human agent.**
  - **R3.1 Participants do not say they would ask for a human at the start.**
    Status: against, for two participants. P4 (Q9, "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it", about the introduction) and P5 (Q10, "I would've asked for a human."). P4 also says in Q5 "I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone" at first. P1 (Q6) mentions that a human could be requested at the beginning but does not say they would ask. P2 and P3 say nothing on the topic.
  - **R3.2 The point at which a request would be made is later than "immediately".**
    Status: weak. Only P4 names a point, the introduction (Q9), which is the earliest point in the scenario. P5 gives no timing in Q10, although Q7 describes a reaction to speaking to an AI assistant "immediately" in a car accident.
  - **R3.3 Stated intentions to ask for a human reflect what participants would do in a live call.**
    Status: no evidence possible (see list below).

- **R4. The quoted material represents all eight interviews.**
  - **R4.1 Every participant's view is available.**
    Status: no evidence possible (see list below).

## Leaf claims for which no evidence is possible

- **R1.3** Satisfaction with voice AI and with traditional voice automation assessed on the same basis for the same participants. The material describes four prerecorded voice AI scenarios and no traditional automation scenario, and it contains no satisfaction ratings. Comparisons in Q1 to Q3 are from memory of earlier experiences.
- **R2.1** Participants learn they are speaking with an AI at an identifiable point. The material does not say whether or when the scenarios disclosed the AI.
- **R2.4 and R3.3** Stated intentions reflect live-call behaviour. Participants listened to prerecorded scenarios, so no one hung up or asked for a human. Every relevant statement is hypothetical ("would've", "if I was").
- **R4.1** Every participant's view is available. P8 and P9 have no quote, and the material says only that some participants are quoted. The basis for choosing the ten quotes is not given.

## Assumptions and limitations

The technique assumed that the three hypotheses can be split into sub-claims that are each necessary, and that interview statements count as evidence for each leaf. It cannot weigh leaves against each other, so the overall reading rests on judgement.

Six of eight participants are quoted, and the quotes are a selection of unknown basis. Counts such as four against three are counts of quoted participants, not of the sample. Silence in a quote is treated as no evidence, not as support. The tree can show which claims lack evidence but cannot supply it, and it cannot check the transcripts or scenario scripts, which would settle R2.1 and R1.2b.

## Alternative explanations

The split between participants may reflect context, not attitude to voice AI. The two strongest statements about hanging up or asking for a human come from P5 about a car accident (Q7, Q10) and P10 about an introduction judged too long (Q8). Stress and introduction length, not the AI itself, could be driving them. This would leave H2 and H3 undecided for ordinary calls.

The pattern could also be an artefact of listening to recordings. Participants who rated the AI favourably (P1, P2, P3) did not discuss hanging up or asking for a human, while those who did (P4, P5, P10) were answering what they would do. The favourable and unfavourable groups may differ in the question being answered, not in how they feel. P4 shows the two can coexist: Q5 calls the process "a really good process" while Q9 places a request for a human at the introduction.

# Voice AI interviews: four themes read against H1 to H3

Reflexive thematic analysis of the ten quotes (Q1 to Q10). Only six of the eight participants are quoted (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P10). P8 and P9 have no extracts in the material, so nothing is said about them. The themes are patterns of meaning in this sample only.

## Theme 1: Fluency and human-likeness are what earns approval

**Description.** Favourable reactions are explained by how the AI compares with something worse the participant has already met. The AI is judged by whether it sounds like a person, asks the right questions and spares the caller repetition. The reference point differs: a keyword-matching chatbot, a robotic voice, or the experience of repeating oneself.

**Data extracts.**
- Q1 (P1): "This AI definitely seems a bit more, uh, advanced." P1 contrasts it with earlier chatbots that "just parsed, um, articles from their own website" and concludes "this one seems to be pretty dynamic."
- Q2 (P2): "It seemed like talking to a real person." P2 adds that it "knew exactly what it needed to ask."
- Q3 (P3): "that was really excellent. It was like really seamless." P3 contrasts it with having "to repeat yourself and stuff."

## Theme 2: Initial resistance driven by prior experience, which may soften

**Description.** Some participants arrive wary because of earlier encounters with AI agents. For P4 the wariness is described as lifting as the interaction proceeds. For P1 it shows as annoyance, and the remedy P1 mentions is an early offer of a human.

**Data extracts.**
- Q5 (P4): "at first. I mean, if it was myself, I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone, but then as the process goes on, you realise it's actually, um, a really good process."
- Q6 (P1): "I definitely felt, um. I felt a little bit annoyed 'cause I've had pre uh, previous experiences with AI agents especially..."

## Theme 3: Voice quality, setting and length decide tolerance

**Description.** Negative reactions point at specific features of the scenario rather than at AI in general: an American accent, a voice heard as cold, a stressful situation such as a car accident, and an introduction that runs too long. These participants judge the AI against what the moment calls for (local familiarity, warmth, speed).

**Data extracts.**
- Q4 (P10): "First of all, this sounds very much like an AI voice. Um, and second of all, it's American. So I want, you know, that local experience."
- Q7 (P5): "if I was in a car accident and then immediately spoke to an AI assistant, I would be extremely frustrated... It's a stressful environment and AI in its current state, and especially with the, the voice that's been decided to be used in that scenario as very cold in clinical."
- Q8 (P10): "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro. This one? At the intro. Okay. Yeah, it was way too long."

## Theme 4: The introduction is where leaving or escalating is imagined

**Description.** Where participants describe exiting, they place it at the start of the call. Both the human request and the hang up are stated as hypotheticals about what they would do, since the scenarios were prerecorded and no participant is quoted as actually doing either. P5 describes the human request as a first step and hanging up as a fallback.

**Data extracts.**
- Q9 (P4): "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it" (said about asking for a human at the introduction).
- Q10 (P5): "I would've asked for a human. Yeah. If I didn't get that, then. I probably would've hung up and then tried to do it manually online."
- Q8 (P10), also under Theme 3: "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro."
- Q6 (P1), also under Theme 2: P1 recalls that "if you wanted to, um, get a human. Agent on the line, you could as well at the beginning."

## Written account

The extracts do not support the three hypotheses evenly. They also do not support them as a set. The clearest pattern is that reactions depend on what the AI is compared with. Themes 1 and 3 show the same participants and quotes pulling in opposite directions depending on the reference point. Against clunky chatbots, robotic voices and repeating oneself, the AI is praised (Q1, Q2, Q3). Against what a stressful or local-service moment needs, it is criticised (Q4, Q7, Q8).

H1 (voice AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation) has partial and indirect support. Three participants speak well of the AI. However, none of the three compares it with traditional voice automation in the sense of a phone menu or interactive voice response system. P1 compares it with website chatbots, P2 with a robotic-sounding voice, and P3 with a repetitive experience that could be of either kind. The material also holds contrary reactions (Q4, Q7) that are not comparisons with automation at all. Satisfaction is therefore suggested for some participants, and the material cannot confirm the comparison the hypothesis states.

H2 (customers do not hang up immediately when they learn they are speaking with an AI) is contradicted for two participants, in stated intention only. P10 says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro" (Q8) and P5 would hang up if no human were offered (Q10). The reasons given differ in kind. P10 cites the length of the introduction, which is not about the AI disclosure itself. P5's hang up is conditional on being refused a human. No quoted participant says they hung up on learning it was an AI. The material supports "some participants say they would leave early" and does not support or contradict the hypothesis as worded, which is about the moment of learning.

H3 (customers do not immediately ask for a human) is also contradicted for two participants in stated intention. P4 would probably ask at the introduction (Q9) and P5 would ask for a human (Q10). Q5 suggests P4's preference fades as the call proceeds, and P1's annoyance (Q6) was tied to the human option being offered at the start. In this sample, wanting a human appears to be a first reaction that a good process may relieve, which is the reverse of the hypothesis for those participants.

Read together, the introduction is the pivot. Early on, participants imagine asking for a human or hanging up (Q8, Q9, Q10). Later, the same kind of participant reports a good process (Q5). The evidence for H2 and H3 is therefore about the first moments, and the evidence for H1 is about the experience as a whole. These are different points in the call, so they should not be netted off against each other.

For the decision this informs, the safest reading is that the sample does not show customers accepting the AI at the outset. It shows approval that depends on fluency, voice and a short, well-placed introduction, and it shows that a route to a human matters to some participants from the first seconds.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The method assumes the extracts are interpretable in the form given. Only ten quotes from six of eight participants are available, with no surrounding transcript, so each theme rests on one to three extracts. The themes are provisional and neither saturated nor checked against the full set.
- Reflexive analysis normally works from the researcher's complete familiarisation with the data. That phase could only be done on the supplied quotes. Unquoted material, including everything from P8 and P9, could change or contradict these themes.
- The method does not test hypotheses. The verdicts above are interpretive readings of the extracts and not tests.
- No counts are given as findings, in line with the method. Naming which participants said what is not a measure of how common a view is.
- Participants reacted to prerecorded scenarios. Statements about hanging up or asking for a human are reported intentions, not observed behaviour, and the material does not say which of the four scenarios each quote refers to.
- The material does not say how the AI's nature was disclosed, so the "when they learn" wording of H2 cannot be examined directly.

## Alternative explanations

- The positive reactions (Q1, Q2, Q3) and the negative ones (Q4, Q7, Q8) may reflect different scenarios the participants were responding to, not different customer attitudes. Q7 refers to a car accident, which points to the motor claim scenario. The material does not say which scenarios the other quotes concern, so scenario type could explain the split.
- The material is not ordered and the quoted subset is selective. The apparent contrast between enthusiasts and sceptics may follow from which quotes were chosen, not from a real division among the eight participants.
- Individual differences may matter more than the AI's features. P1 appears in both a favourable theme (Q1) and an annoyed one (Q6), which suggests one person can hold both views, and that the "positive" and "negative" groupings are about the quotes rather than about types of customer.
- The wish for a human (Q5, Q9, Q10) may be a general preference for human service in stressful or consequential calls, and not a reaction to this particular AI.

# Framework matrix of eight interviews on voice AI customer support

## Themes (columns)

The columns follow the three hypotheses, plus one theme that emerged from the quotes.

- T1, satisfaction and comparison with earlier automation (H1)
- T2, hanging up on learning it is an AI (H2)
- T3, asking for a human agent (H3)
- T4, voice and naturalness (emerged from the quotes)

## Matrix

Each cell summarises only the quotes shown in the material. "No coded data" means the material has no quote that fits the theme for that participant. It does not mean the participant held no view.

| Case | T1 Satisfaction and comparison | T2 Hanging up | T3 Asking for a human | T4 Voice and naturalness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Q1: finds this AI "a bit more, uh, advanced" and "pretty dynamic", compared with earlier chat bots that parsed website articles ("Like those never work"). Q6: "a little bit annoyed" because of previous experiences with AI agents. Both comparisons are with earlier chat bots and AI agents, not voice automation. | No coded data. | Q6: recalls that "if you wanted to, um, get a human. Agent on the line, you could as well at the beginning". The quote does not say whether P1 would ask for one. | No coded data. |
| P2 | Q2: "It seemed like talking to a real person" and "it knew exactly what it needed to ask". Contrasted with a "robot voice" from other systems. | No coded data. | No coded data. | Q2: did not sound like a robot voice. |
| P3 | Q3: "really excellent" and "really seamless", with no need to repeat yourself, which P3 contrasts with previous experiences. | No coded data. | No coded data. | Q3: "kind of like he was talking to an actual person". |
| P4 | Q5: after a hesitant start, "you realise it's actually, um, a really good process". | No coded data. | Q5: "at first" would "probably" want to speak to someone. Q9: "that's probably where I would do it", said about asking for a human at the introduction. Both are hypothetical. | No coded data. |
| P5 | Q7: would be "extremely frustrated" if in a car accident and speaking to an AI assistant (hypothetical, motor claim scenario). | Q10: "I probably would've hung up" if a human was not provided, then would try online. Conditional on the human request failing. | Q10: "I would've asked for a human." | Q7: the voice is "very cold in clinical". |
| P8 | No coded data. | No coded data. | No coded data. | No coded data. |
| P9 | No coded data. | No coded data. | No coded data. | No coded data. |
| P10 | Q4: wants a "local experience" because the voice is American. Q8: the introduction was "way too long". No comparison with earlier automation is given. | Q8: "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro." The stated reason is the length of the introduction. | No coded data. | Q4: "this sounds very much like an AI voice". |

## Empty cells

- P8 and P9 have no coded data in any column. The material gives no quote from either, so the matrix cannot place them.
- T2 is empty for P1, P2, P3, P4, P8 and P9. Only P5 and P10 have anything coded for hanging up.
- T3 is empty for P2, P3, P8, P9 and P10. P1's cell holds a mention of the human option, not a request for one.
- T1 has no direct comparison with traditional voice automation in any cell. The comparators in the quotes are chat bots (P1), a "robot voice" (P2), having to repeat yourself (P3) and AI agents (P1).

## Reading across the rows (cases)

- P1 is mixed on its own. Q1 is positive about this AI, while Q6 records annoyance linked to earlier experiences and the human-agent option.
- P2 and P3 are the only rows that are positive across all their coded cells, and both mention that it felt like a real person. Neither has any data on hanging up or asking for a human.
- P4 starts hesitant and ends positive, and holds both a want to speak to someone (Q5) and a possible request for a human at the introduction (Q9).
- P5 and P10 are the rows with hang-up data. In both, the stated trigger is something other than the bare fact of speaking to an AI: a failed request for a human (P5, Q10) and the length of the introduction (P10, Q8).
- P8 and P9 contribute nothing.

## Reading down the columns (themes)

- T1 (H1): the quoted positive reactions (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5) are all comparisons with something other than traditional voice automation, or are within-scenario judgements. The material cannot show that participants found this more satisfying than traditional voice automation. The negative quotes (Q4, Q6, Q7) are about context, voice or earlier experience.
- T2 (H2): the only quotes about hanging up (Q8, Q10) describe hanging up as something P10 would have done and P5 might have done. No quote shows a participant continuing after learning it is an AI, apart from P4's account of moving from hesitation to approval (Q5), which is not about hanging up. The material does not support H2 and has one direct counterexample (Q8).
- T3 (H3): two participants say they would, or probably would, ask for a human (P4, P5). No quote shows a participant who would not ask. Q5 and Q9 describe an initial impulse that P4 says passed. The material does not support H3, and it leans against it for P4 and P5.
- T4 (emerged): the voice is mentioned in four rows and splits by direction. P2 and P3 read it as human-like, and P5 and P10 read it as cold, clinical or too obviously AI.

## What the matrix shows and does not show

Within this sample, the quotes link hanging up and asking for a human to the scenario and the introduction (Q7, Q8, Q9, Q10), and link positive reactions to the voice sounding human-like (Q2, Q3). The matrix does not show how many of the eight participants hold each view. The cells are coded summaries of selected quotes, so the number of filled cells must not be read as a count of responses. For a decision, treat H1 as untested against its stated comparator, H2 as not supported with one contrary quote, and H3 as not supported, with two participants who lean against it.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumed that the ten quotes are a fair record of each participant's views. The material says only some participants are quoted and gives no basis for how they were chosen, so the matrix may under-represent views.
- It assumed that the quotes can be coded against themes without the full transcripts. Several cells rest on a single quote, and Q9 and Q10 are hypothetical statements about what the participant would have done.
- The technique is built for an experienced qualitative lead working from full coded transcripts. With ten quotes it works as an audit trail of what is and is not in the material, not as a full framework analysis.
- Q9 is a short fragment whose meaning depends on the bracketed note. Q6 is ambiguous about whether P1 would ask for a human.
- The material does not say which of the four scenarios each quote refers to, apart from the motor claim reference in Q7. Differences between scenarios cannot be separated from differences between people.
- T4 was added by the analyst from the quotes. It is not one of the hypotheses.

## Alternative explanations

- The pattern in T2 and T3 may reflect scenario stress rather than a general attitude to AI. P5's reactions (Q7, Q10) are tied to a car accident, and P10's hang-up (Q8) is tied to the length of the introduction. Under this reading, hanging up and asking for a human depend on the situation and the introduction design, and the hypotheses H2 and H3 are too broad to test as stated.
- The positive T1 quotes may reflect the voice quality of the prerecorded scenarios rather than satisfaction with voice AI in general. P2 and P3 both praise how human it sounded, while P5 and P10 object to the voice, so the voice may be the driver in both directions.
- The empty T2 and T3 cells for most participants may reflect what the interviewer asked or what was selected for quoting, not an absence of views. A different selection of quotes could change the reading of H2 and H3.

# Content analysis of eight voice AI interviews against H1 to H3

## Coding scheme and method

The unit of analysis is one quote (Q1 to Q10). A quote can receive more than one code. Codes were set in advance from the wording of the three hypotheses, plus two categories that emerged from the material (E1, E2). One coder (this analysis) applied the scheme, so there is no agreement check, and the counts below are not reliability-tested.

Counts are only over the ten supplied quotes from six participants (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P10). P8 and P9 have no quotes in the material, so they are uncoded and their views are unknown. A participant who is not quoted on a topic is not counted as holding a view on it.

## Category frequencies

| Code | Category | Quotes coded | Quote count | Participants | Participant count |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H1a | Favourable view of the AI interaction | Q1, Q2, Q3, Q5 (second half) | 4 | P1, P2, P3, P4 | 4 |
| H1b | Unfavourable view of the AI interaction | Q4, Q6, Q7, Q8 | 4 | P1, P5, P10 | 3 |
| H1c | Favourable comparison with earlier automation | Q1, Q2, Q3 | 3 | P1, P2, P3 | 3 |
| H2a | Says they would have hung up | Q8, Q10 (conditional) | 2 | P5, P10 | 2 |
| H2b | Says they would stay on the call | none | 0 | none | 0 |
| H3a | Says they would ask, or want to ask, for a human | Q5 (first half), Q9, Q10 | 3 | P4, P5 | 2 |
| H3b | Notes a human option existed, no request | Q6 | 1 | P1 | 1 |
| E1 | Objection to voice quality or character | Q4, Q7 | 2 | P5, P10 | 2 |
| E2 | The introduction named as the trigger point | Q8, Q9 | 2 | P4, P10 | 2 |

Coding notes that affect the counts:

- Q5 is coded twice. "at first" the speaker would want to speak to someone (H3a), and later calls it "a really good process" (H1a).
- P1 appears in both H1a (Q1) and H1b (Q6), so participant counts for H1a and H1b overlap and must not be added.
- Q4 is coded unfavourable because the speaker objects to the AI voice and its American accent. It does not state dissatisfaction in those words.
- Q9 and Q10 are not coded on H1, because neither expresses an evaluation of the interaction.
- Q2 and Q3 are coded as favourable comparisons because they contrast the AI with a "robot voice" and with having "to repeat yourself". Q1 compares it with "chat bots", which are text tools and not voice automation.

## What the frequencies show for each hypothesis

**H1: more satisfying than traditional voice automation.** Mixed within this sample. Three participants (P1, P2, P3) compare the AI favourably with earlier systems, and P4 comes round to it. Three participants (P1, P5, P10) express dissatisfaction. No quote uses the word "satisfying", and none compares the AI with a traditional voice automation (IVR) system by name. The closest comparisons are Q2 (robot voice) and Q3 (having to repeat yourself). Q1's comparison is with chatbots. The material therefore shows a link between favourable views and comparison with earlier tools, but it does not show that the AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation. Two of the unfavourable views (Q7, Q4) concern voice character and a stressful context, which the favourable quotes do not address.

**H2: customers do not hang up immediately on learning they are speaking with an AI.** Not tested directly. No quote reports a hang up, and none says a participant hung up on learning it was an AI. Two quotes state a hang up intention. Q8 ("I would've definitely have hung up at the intro") gives length of the introduction as the reason, not the AI disclosure. Q10 makes hanging up conditional on not getting a human. The material does not say whether the introduction is where the AI is disclosed. Evidence against H2 is therefore weak and indirect: two of six quoted participants say they would have hung up, under conditions that do not match the hypothesis wording. No participant says the opposite.

**H3: customers do not immediately ask for a human agent.** Counter-evidence exists. P4 says (Q5) that at first they would want to speak to someone, and Q9 says "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it", said about asking for a human at the introduction. P5 says in Q10 "I would've asked for a human". That is two of six quoted participants, with three quotes. P4's later reassurance (Q5) shows the wish can fade as the call proceeds. All of these are stated intentions after listening to prerecorded scenarios, not observed behaviour, so none shows an actual request. No quote shows a participant choosing not to ask.

## Pattern across codes

H3a and H2a overlap on P5 (Q10), and E2 overlaps with both through P4 and P10. Taken together, the codes that bear on hanging up and requesting a human cluster at the introduction (Q8, Q9) and at P5's accident scenario (Q7, Q10). The favourable codes (H1a, H1c) come from P1, P2, P3 and P4, none of whom state an intention to hang up or ask for a human, other than P4's first reaction in Q5. This is an association within six participants only.

## Agreement between coders

Not applicable. Only one coder was used, so no agreement statistic is reported, and the borderline codings above (Q4, Q5, Q6, Q8) are unchecked judgements.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumes a coding scheme fixed before reading. The scheme here was derived from the hypotheses and so tends to find material that matches them. Two emergent codes (E1, E2) were added after reading.
- Counting assumes each quote is a comparable unit. The quotes are selected extracts ("Only some participants are quoted") in no particular order, so frequencies measure the selected quotes, not how often each view arose across the interviews.
- P8 and P9 have no quotes, so the counts cover six of the eight participants. Absence of a quote is not absence of a view.
- Coding removes context. Q7 is hypothetical (a car accident), Q8 and Q10 are conditional, and Q5 changes over time. A single category label hides these differences, so the table should be read alongside the quote text.
- The material cannot answer whether any participant hung up or asked for a human in practice, whether the AI disclosure falls in the introduction, or how participants rated traditional voice automation.
- No coder agreement check was possible, and no significance can be claimed from ten quotes.

## Alternative explanations

- The favourable and unfavourable views may reflect different scenarios heard, not different attitudes to voice AI. Each participant heard four scenarios, but the material does not say which scenario each quote refers to. Q7 is about a motor claim and could differ from views on sales or cancellation.
- The hang up and human-request codes may reflect dislike of a long introduction (Q8, Q9) more than dislike of AI. If so, H2 and H3 would be affected by the design of the introduction, not by the AI disclosure.
- The favourable quotes (Q1 to Q3) may be favourable because the participants' expectations were low from earlier chatbot experience, so the AI improves on a low baseline without being more satisfying than voice automation.
- Participants may state hypothetical intentions more strongly than they would act. The stated hang up and human-request intentions could therefore overstate real behaviour, which would weaken the counter-evidence to H2 and H3.

The result describes these quotes only and cannot support any rate or percentage claim beyond the counts above.
- Participants P8 and P9 are not quoted, so the table cannot say whether they support or oppose anything. The quotes were selected by the compiler, and selection may over-represent strong reactions.

- P1 holding both stances (Q1 and Q6) suggests that stance may depend on which aspect is discussed (conversation quality versus intro or escalation options) and not on a fixed personal position.
- Favourable H1 statements may reflect comparison with a poor earlier experience (chatbots, robot voice) and not satisfaction with voice AI itself.

# Preprocessing sensitivity test on the eight interviews

## Question and what was counted

The brief asks whether the interviews support H1 (voice AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation), H2 (customers do not hang up immediately on learning it is an AI) and H3 (customers do not immediately ask for a human). The technique converts the ten quotes (Q1 to Q10, six of the eight participants: P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P10; P8 and P9 have no quote in the material) into countable tokens and re-runs one result under six cleaning regimes. Nothing here exceeds patterns within this sample.

The main result tested is a fixed cue lexicon, written before counting, applied to each quote. The lexicon is matched on word starts so that stemming does not break it.

- H1 positive cues: seamless, excellent, advanced, dynamic, real, actual, easy, exactly, good.
- H1 negative cues: annoy, frustrat, cold, clinical, robot, long.
- H2 cue: hung, hang.
- H3 cues: human, someone.

The result is the number of quotes (out of 10) containing each cue group, plus the top five terms by frequency. Code was Python 3 with only the standard library. No tokeniser or stopword package was installed, so a regular expression tokeniser and a hand-written English stopword list were used. The suffix stemmer is crude (it turns "seamless" into "seamles" and "process" into "proces"), which is why cues are matched by prefix.

## Log of cleaning rules

Every regime starts with these rules: curly apostrophes made straight; quote text only (the ID and participant code are excluded); tokens are runs of letters and apostrophes; single-character tokens dropped; Q1 to Q10 treated as ten separate documents.

| Rule | R1 | R2 | R3 | R4 | R5 | R6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercase | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Stopword removal (about 120 function words, includes not, no, nor, didn't) | no | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Negations (not, no, nor, never, didn't) kept despite stopword removal | not applicable | no | no | no | yes | yes |
| Suffix stemming (ingly, edly, ing, ed, ly, es, s when 4 or more letters remain) | no | no | yes | yes | no | yes |
| Transcript fillers and hedges removed (um, uh, like, yeah, okay, kind, stuff, really, you, know, definitely, probably, sometimes, actually, seems, seemed, think, just) | no | no | no | yes | no | yes |

Negation tokens occur in only four quotes (never in Q1; didn't in Q2, Q3 and Q10), so the R5 and R6 choice changed only the vocabulary size by 3 tokens each and no cue count.

## What the cue quotes say when read

Counting is only a locator. Reading the matched quotes changes how they should be used.

- H1: Q1 contrasts the AI with older chatbots ("this one seems to be pretty dynamic"), Q2 says it "seemed like talking to a real person" and Q3 says "that was really excellent". These three (P1, P2, P3) favour the AI. Q5 (P4) starts reluctant and ends positive ("a really good process"). The negative cue in Q2 is the word "robot" used in a comparison, so the lexicon wrongly counts Q2 as negative. Q6 (P1), Q7 (P5) and Q8 (P10) are unfavourable. Q4 (P10) matched no cue but says "this sounds very much like an AI voice". No quote compares satisfaction with traditional voice automation directly; Q1 compares with website chatbots, which is a different thing. H1 is only partly addressed.
- H2: Q8 and Q10 are the only hang cues, from P10 and P5. Both are hypothetical ("I would've definitely have hung up at the intro."; "I probably would've hung up and then tried to do it manually online."). No quote reports an actual hang-up. The cue count of 2 shows two of six quoted participants state they would hang up, so H2 is contradicted for those two and untested for P1, P2, P3 and P4.
- H3: Q5, Q9 and Q10 are the human-request cues that matter. P4 says "I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone" and, about the introduction, "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it". P5 says "I would've asked for a human." Q6 (P1) matched "human" but reports that a human option was offered, not a request. So two of six quoted participants (P4, P5) say they would ask for a human at or near the start, and H3 is contradicted for them.

## Whether themes or rankings changed across regimes

The cue counts did not change: every cell is identical across R1 to R6, so the link between quotes and each hypothesis is stable to these cleaning choices. The word-frequency ranking did change. The top five in R1 are function words, in R2 to R3 are dominated by the fillers "um" and "like", and only from R4 (fillers removed) does a substantive set (ai, voice, talk) appear. Rankings of raw frequent words are therefore unstable and should not be used for themes here; the fixed cue lexicon is stable.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The lexicon was chosen by me from reading the ten quotes, so it fits this sample by construction. Stable counts across regimes show insensitivity to cleaning, not that the lexicon is valid.
- Bag-of-words ignores tense, conditionals and contrast. It cannot separate a hypothetical hang-up from a real one, a request from a noted option (Q6), or "robot" in praise from "robot" in complaint (Q2).
- Ten short quotes is too little text for an unsupervised model, so none was run. Whether neural embedding methods are equally sensitive to cleaning was not tested.
- The stemmer and stopword list were home-made because no package was installed. Different standard lists could differ, though the negation test suggests little effect on the cues.
- Quotes were selected from the transcripts ("only some participants are quoted"), and P8 and P9 have no quote. Counts are of quotes, not of participants' views, and say nothing about the full interviews or about customers generally.
- The technique cannot say which hypothesis is more true; it only shows the cue pattern is not an artefact of cleaning.

## Alternative explanations

- The stable cue counts may reflect how the quotes were selected, not how the participants felt. A reader who picked quotes to illustrate both sides would produce the same near-even split (four positive cue quotes, four negative cue quotes) regardless of cleaning.
- The two hang-up cues (P10, P5) may reflect scenario content rather than AI itself: Q7 ties P5's reaction to a car accident and Q8 ties P10's to a long introduction and an American accent. The pattern could be about the introduction and the voice, not about learning it is an AI.
- Q5 suggests the human-request cue may be a first impression that fades as the call proceeds, so "immediately" in H3 and H2 may be met for some participants even where a human was initially wanted.

# Analysis of competing hypotheses: voice AI customer support interviews

## Hypotheses

The material gives three hypotheses. They are not mutually exclusive, so each is rated on its own against the evidence. Because the list may be incomplete, one rival hypothesis (H4) is added by the analyst. It is not in the material.

- H1: Customers find voice AI interactions more satisfying than traditional voice automation.
- H2: Customers do not hang up immediately when they learn they are speaking with an AI.
- H3: Customers do not immediately ask for a human agent.
- H4 (added): Reactions depend on the participant and the situation (for example stress, the voice used, the length of the introduction), so none of H1 to H3 describes the sample as a whole.

## Rating key

- C: consistent with the hypothesis
- I: inconsistent with the hypothesis
- N: neutral, not diagnostic, or the quote does not address it

## Matrix

| Evidence | Participant | Gist | H1 | H2 | H3 | H4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | P1 | More advanced and dynamic than earlier chatbots | C (weak) | N | N | N |
| Q2 | P2 | Like talking to a real person, not a robot voice | C | N | N | N |
| Q3 | P3 | "really excellent", "really seamless" | C | N | N | N |
| Q4 | P10 | Sounds like an AI and American, wants a local experience | I (weak) | N | N | C |
| Q5 | P4 | Would first want to speak to someone, then finds the process good | C | C (weak) | I | C |
| Q6 | P1 | "a little bit annoyed" from previous AI agent experiences | N | N | N | C (weak) |
| Q7 | P5 | Would be "extremely frustrated" in a car accident; voice "very cold in clinical" | I | N | N | C |
| Q8 | P10 | "would've definitely have hung up at the intro" | I | I | N | C |
| Q9 | P4 | Would ask for a human at the introduction | N | N | I | C |
| Q10 | P5 | "I would've asked for a human" | I (weak) | N | I | C |

## Notes on the ratings

- Q1 compares the AI with earlier chatbots, not with traditional voice automation, so its support for H1 is indirect. Q2 and Q3 contrast the AI with robot-sounding or repetitive systems, which is closer to H1 but still a reaction to one scenario.
- Q4 is rated weakly inconsistent with H1 because the stated concerns (AI sounding voice, American accent) are reasons for lower satisfaction. P10 does not say whether the interaction was satisfying overall.
- Q5 is rated consistent with H2 only weakly. P4 says the process improved over time, which suggests staying on the call, but it is a retrospective reaction to a prerecorded scenario.
- Q6 is ambiguous. The annoyance is linked to "previous experiences with AI agents", and it is not clear whether it refers to the scenarios heard. The remark about being offered a human at the beginning is not a request for one.
- Q10 is rated weakly inconsistent with H1 as a signal of dissatisfaction. The hang up in Q10 is conditional on not getting a human and follows a request, so it is not rated against H2.
- All of Q4 to Q10 are what participants say they would do. The material does not show any participant actually hanging up or asking for a human.

## Evidence that discriminates between hypotheses

- Q8 is the only item rated inconsistent with H2. It also counts against H1.
- Q5, Q9 and Q10 are rated inconsistent with H3. Q5 and Q9 come from P4 and Q10 from P5, so the inconsistency rests on two participants.
- Q7 and Q4 separate H1 from H4. They show negative reactions that H1 does not accommodate but H4 does.
- Q1, Q2 and Q3 favour H1 but do not distinguish H1 from H4, because H4 allows some participants to be satisfied.
- Q6 does not discriminate.

## Inconsistency count

| Hypothesis | Consistent | Inconsistent | Neutral |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | 4 | 4 (3 clear or weak on dissatisfaction, 1 weak) | 2 |
| H2 | 1 (weak) | 1 | 8 |
| H3 | 0 | 3 | 7 |
| H4 | 8 | 0 | 2 |

The inconsistency counts for H1 include Q4 and Q10 as weak ratings. Excluding them, H1 has two inconsistencies (Q7, Q8).

## Result

H4 has the fewest inconsistencies (none), but it is the least testable hypothesis, because it predicts that reactions vary and so it is consistent with almost any pattern. Among the three stated hypotheses, H2 has the fewest inconsistencies (one, Q8), but it also has the least evidence, with eight of ten items neutral. H3 has three inconsistencies from two participants (P4 and P5) and is the hypothesis the sample most clearly counts against. H1 has support from P1, P2 and P3 and counter-evidence from P4, P5 and P10, so the sample is split.

Within this sample, the interviews do not support H3, give mixed evidence on H1, and give little evidence on H2 either way (P10 is the single counter-case).

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumes each quote is an independent piece of evidence. Q5 and Q9 (P4), Q7 and Q10 (P5), Q4 and Q8 (P10) and Q1 and Q6 (P1) come from the same people, so the ten items represent fewer independent voices. Counts of C and I overstate the evidence base.
- Only some participants are quoted. P8 and P9 have no quotes, so the matrix cannot say anything about them. The material does not state whether the quotes were selected to illustrate particular views.
- The matrix cannot show how common each view is, because the material gives no complete record of what each participant said.
- Ratings of weak and neutral are judgements by the analyst. A different reader could rate Q1, Q5, Q6 and Q10 differently.
- H4 was added by the analyst to avoid an incomplete hypothesis list. It was not specified in the brief.
- The material cannot tell whether any participant actually learned they were speaking with an AI during a live call, since the scenarios were prerecorded. H2 and H3 are therefore tested only through stated intentions.
- "Traditional voice automation" is not described in the material, so H1 cannot be tested as a comparison.

## Alternative explanations

- Hypothetical scenario framing: the negative reactions in Q7 to Q10 are about imagined situations such as a car accident or a long introduction. Participants may predict stronger reactions than they would show in practice, which would weaken the case against H2 and H3.
- Scenario and voice effects: the difference between P1 to P3 (positive) and P4, P5 and P10 (negative or conditional) may reflect the scenario each person was thinking of (Q7 refers to a motor accident) or the voice (Q4, Q7) and not a general view of voice AI. This is the H4 reading.
- Introduction length as the main driver: Q8 and Q9 both point to the introduction, and Q6 mentions the offer of a human at the beginning. The pattern may be about the opening of the call, not about AI as such.
- Prior experience: Q1 and Q6 both mention earlier AI experiences, so satisfaction may depend on what each participant compared the scenarios with.
results.TC1-16:
# Disconfirmation search on the favoured reading of the voice AI interviews

## Claim under test

The eight result files agree closely enough to give one favoured reading. It is stated here precisely, as patterns within this sample only (six of eight participants are quoted: P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P10).

- C1. H1 is partly supported. P1, P2 and P3 speak well of the AI, but no quote compares it with traditional voice automation, so the comparison in H1 cannot be tested.
- C2. H2 is neither supported nor clearly refuted. P10 (Q8) and P5 (Q10) say they would hang up, but their stated reasons are the length of the introduction and not getting a human, not learning that it is an AI.
- C3. H3 is contradicted by P4 (Q9) and P5 (Q10), as stated intentions only.
- C4. The differences between participants are better explained by context (stress, voice, introduction length, earlier experience) than by attitude to voice AI as such, and every hang-up or human-request statement is hypothetical.

## Evidence that would refute the claim, written before searching

The following list was written before the search below was run. It was written after the eight result files had been read, so it is not blind to the favoured reading. Each item is stated so that finding it would count against a named part of the claim.

- D1. A quote in which a participant compares the voice AI with an interactive voice response system or phone menu and prefers or dislikes it. This would contradict the part of C1 that says H1 cannot be tested.
- D2. A quote in which a participant says they would stay on, or did stay on, the call after learning it is an AI. This would contradict the part of C2 that says H2 has no support.
- D3. A quote in which a participant links hanging up, frustration or a request for a human to the fact that it is an AI, rather than to length, setting or a refused request. This would contradict the attribution in C2 and C4.
- D4. A quote in which the objection arises without stress, long introduction or refused request. This would contradict the context explanation in C4.
- D5. A quote reporting that someone actually hung up or actually asked for a human. This would contradict the "hypothetical only" part of C3 and C4.
- D6. A quote showing that P4 or P5 would not ask for a human at the start. This would contradict C3.
- D7. A quote from P8 or P9, or a statement of how the ten quotes were chosen. Either could overturn the reading, in either direction.
- D8. A statement in the findings that the material does not support. This would show that the favoured reading rests on something other than the quotes.

## Search used

The search covered all ten quotes (Q1 to Q10) and the eight result files in full, not a sample of them. Two passes were made. The first was a read of every quote against each item above. The second was a text search of the material for terms that would signal each item, chosen to include terms that favour the opposite of the claim: IVR, menu, press, automat, robot, stay, stayed, continue, carry on, hung, hang, human, someone, AI, intro, local, satisf, scenario, claim, accident and immediately. The terms were run against the material, and the result files were then checked for statements that go beyond what those matches show. The search is limited to this material. No transcript, scenario script or participant outside the ten quotes was available.

## Results

| Item | Found or not found | Search used |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Not found as stated. Partly found for voice: Q2 | Terms IVR, menu, press and automat returned nothing in the quotes. Q2 returned "robot". Read Q1, Q2, Q3 for any named earlier system. |
| D2 | Partly found: Q5 | Terms stay, stayed, continue and carry on returned nothing. Read all quotes from P1 to P4 for a statement about remaining on the call. |
| D3 | Partly found: Q7, Q4 | Searched "AI" in every quote and read each hang-up and human-request quote for its stated reason. |
| D4 | Found: Q4, Q6 | Read each negative quote (Q4, Q6, Q7, Q8) for a trigger other than stress, introduction length or a refused request. |
| D5 | Not found | Searched hung, hang, human and someone, then read each match for tense. All matches are conditional or hypothetical. |
| D6 | Partly found: Q9, Q5 | Read Q5, Q9 and Q10 for any hedge on whether the request would be made, and for timing. |
| D7 | Not found | Searched for P8, P9 and for any selection rule. The material says only that some participants are quoted. |
| D8 | Found: scenario attribution, and two overstatements in the findings | Compared each factual claim in the eight files with the quote text. |

### D1: comparison with traditional voice automation. Not found, with one partial hit

No quote names an interactive voice response system, a phone menu or press-a-button automation. The closest is Q2, where P2 says "sometimes when you are talking to a more of a robot, it sounds more like a robot voice". That is a comparison with a robot-sounding voice, which could be a voice system. Q1 compares with chat bots, which are text tools, and Q3 refers only to the experience of having to "repeat yourself".

This does not refute C1, but it softens it. H1 is not untestable for everyone. P2 gives one indirect voice comparison, and the findings that say no quote compares at all (HE1-13, HE1-14, HE1-15) overstate the gap.

### D2: staying on the call. Partly found

No quote says "I would stay" or "I stayed". Q5 is the nearest. P4 says "at first. I mean, if it was myself, I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone, but then as the process goes on, you realise it's actually, um, a really good process." This describes someone who went through the whole process. It does not say anything about hanging up, and it is a reaction to a prerecorded scenario.

The partial hit gives C2 a small amount of support from P4 that DM-02 and CM1-05 do not record. TC1-13 rates Q5 weakly consistent with H2, which is the fairer reading. C2 should say "neither supported nor clearly refuted, with one weak supporting quote".

### D3: attribution to the fact that it is an AI. Partly found

Two quotes tie the reaction to the AI itself. In Q7, P5 says "if I was in a car accident and then immediately spoke to an AI assistant, I would be extremely frustrated" and adds "AI in its current state". The frustration is attributed to speaking to an AI assistant as well as to the stressful setting. In Q4, P10 says "this sounds very much like an AI voice". P10 does not link this to the hang-up in Q8, and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed.

This weakens the part of C2 and C4 that treats the AI disclosure as not the cause. The findings (CM1-05, HE1-13, HE1-14) say reservations are about context and delivery, "not about the AI". Q7 does not support that wording. The disclosure cannot be ruled out as a driver for P5, and for P10 the link between Q4 and Q8 is plausible but unstated.

### D4: objections that arise without stress, length or a refused request. Found

Q4 is an objection to an AI-sounding, American voice, with no stress and no mention of length. Q6 records annoyance that P1 links to "previous experiences with AI agents", with no stated scenario. Neither fits the three triggers named in the context explanation.

C4 holds for P5 (stress, voice) and for P10 in Q8 (length), but not for the whole sample. Voice character and earlier experience are separate drivers. The context explanation should be stated as several drivers and not as one.

### D5: observed behaviour. Not found

Every relevant quote is hypothetical or conditional: "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro" (Q8), "I would've asked for a human" (Q10), "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it" (Q9). Q6 reports that a human could be requested, which describes what the scenario offered. This part of C3 and C4 stands. The absence is expected, because participants heard prerecorded scenarios, so it does not strengthen the claim on its own.

### D6: P4 or P5 not asking for a human. Partly found

Q9 is hedged twice: "If I was gonna do it" and "probably". The bracketed note naming the introduction as the point is the compiler's, not P4's. Q5 says P4's wish to speak to someone applies "at first" and changes as the process goes on. For P5, Q10 gives no timing, so it does not show an immediate request. In H3, the word that matters is "immediately".

C3 should be softened. For P4, the evidence is a conditional intention that P4 says fades. For P5, it is a request with no stated timing. H3 is contradicted for two participants only in the sense that they say they might ask, and the quotes do not show that they would ask immediately. DM-02 (R3.2, "weak") is closest to this. MM-10 and TC1-13 treat P4 and P5 as plain contradictions.

### D7: P8, P9 or a selection rule. Not found

There is no quote from P8 or P9 and no account of how the ten quotes were chosen. This does not support the claim. It means the search could not test the claim against two of eight participants, and the reading may be skewed in either direction by the choice of quotes.

### D8: statements in the findings that the material does not support. Found

- Q7 is described as being about the motor claim scenario (DM-02, CM1-05, MM-10, HE1-13). The material does not say so. Q7 is hypothetical ("if I was in a car accident") and refers to "that scenario". The motor claim lodgement scenario is one of four the participants heard, so the link is a reasonable inference, but it is not recorded in the material. The context explanation for P5 leans on this inference.
- CM1-05 says the participants who object (P4, P5, P10) "all say they would ask for a human or hang up". P4 says "I'd be probably wanting to speak to someone" and, in Q9, hedges. P10 says nothing about asking for a human. Only P10 (Q8) and P5 (Q10) mention hanging up.
- HE1-14 says "No quote shows a participant who would not ask" for a human. That is true, but it counts silence from P1, P2 and P3 as absence of evidence, which is the right reading, and not as absence of a view. It should not be read as support for H3 being false in general.
- The counts differ because the files count different units. DM-02 gives four participants against three on H1, MM-10 gives four quotes against four, and HE1-15 gives three unfavourable participants. These are consistent once the unit is stated. P1 is on both sides.

## What the findings mean for the claim

The search found nothing that overturns the favoured reading. It did find four places where the reading is stated more firmly than the material allows.

- C1 survives with one adjustment. H1 remains partly supported by P1, P2 and P3. The comparison with traditional voice automation is not tested in any quote, except that Q2 offers one indirect voice comparison.
- C2 survives with one adjustment. The disclosure cannot be ruled out as a driver, because P5 names "AI in its current state" in Q7 and P10 names "an AI voice" in Q4. The reasons the findings give (introduction length, a refused human) are the stated reasons, not proven causes. P4's Q5 gives H2 weak support.
- C3 is weaker than most files state. The two participants say they would or probably would ask for a human, but the quotes give no timing for P5, hedge P4 twice, and report intentions only. "Contradicted" should read "contradicted as a stated intention, with timing unconfirmed".
- C4 is only partly borne out. Stress, introduction length and the voice are all named by participants, but Q4 and Q6 show objections that do not fit one context explanation, and the link between Q7 and the motor claim scenario is inferred.

Not finding refuting evidence for D5 and D7 is a result of the material's limits (prerecorded scenarios, six of eight participants quoted, ten selected quotes). It does not confirm the claim. For a decision, the reading is safe as a statement that this sample is split and that some participants want an early route to a human, and it is not safe as a statement about why, or about how many of the eight would act this way.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The list of refuting evidence was written after the eight result files were read. A list written before seeing the favoured reading might have included other items.
- The search covered the ten quotes and the eight result files only. The transcripts and scenario scripts would settle several items (where the AI is disclosed, which scenario each quote refers to, what P8 and P9 said) and were not available.
- Text searches were run on the quote wording, so synonyms not listed (for example "IVR" spelled out, or "press 1") could be missed. Each quote was also read in full to reduce that risk.
- The reading of tense and hedging in Q5, Q9 and Q10 is the analyst's judgement and was not checked by a second reader.
- Ten quotes from six participants cannot support a rate, a percentage or any statement beyond this sample.
- Items marked "partly found" depend on interpretation of short, informal speech with fillers and fragments.

## Alternative explanations

- The partial hits in D1 to D3 may reflect how the quotes were selected. A compiler who chose quotes to show both sides would produce near-even evidence on H1 and some ambiguity on H2 and H3 whatever participants said in full.
- The hedges in Q9 and Q10 may reflect ordinary spoken style, not real uncertainty. Read that way, P4 and P5 would ask for a human early, and the original reading of C3 stands.
- P5 may be reacting to the scenario (a car accident) as the findings say, and the words "AI in its current state" may be incidental. Read that way, D3 does not weaken C2.
- Participants may overstate hypothetical reactions to prerecorded scenarios. This would weaken the contradiction of H2 and H3 further, and it would not support the hypotheses either.
- The favourable group (P1, P2, P3) and the unfavourable group (P4, P5, P10) may differ in the question they were answering, not in their feelings. P4 and P1 each hold both views, which supports this reading.

# Sensitivity of the voice AI interview conclusion to inclusion rules

## What was re-run

The favoured reading, from the eight result files taken together, is this. The interviews do not support H1 to H3 as a set. H1 is split and cannot be tested as a comparison with traditional voice automation. H2 is contradicted by P10 (unconditionally) and P5 (conditionally) in stated intention only. H3 is contradicted by P4 and P5 in stated intention only. Statements about hanging up and asking for a human cluster around the introduction. All of this describes patterns within this sample only.

The technique re-runs the tallies behind that reading while changing one choice at a time. Three tallies are used.

- H1: quoted participants who are favourable against those who are unfavourable about the voice AI, and whether any quote compares it with traditional voice automation.
- H2: quoted participants who say they would hang up.
- H3: quoted participants who say they would ask for a human.

Only six of the eight participants are quoted (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P10). P8 and P9 have no quote, so they are not counted anywhere except in one labelled bounding row.

The uncertain choices, written before re-running, are these: which participant to leave out; whether quotes or participants are the unit; whether hypothetical statements count; whether hedged statements ("probably", "if I was") count; whether P4's later approval cancels the early wish for a human; whether "immediately" requires a stated timing; whether H2 requires that the cause is learning it is an AI; how to code P1 and P4, who speak on both sides; whether context-specific complaints count against the AI; whether the comparator in H1 must be voice automation; and whether the text-cleaning choices in PE-02 change the cue counts.

Some of these choices weaken the favoured reading and some strengthen it. The rows that weaken it are included deliberately, because the favoured reading is the one being tested.

## Sensitivity table

Each row changes one thing. The original row is first.

| 21 | Combined: rows 10, 11, 12 and 13 together, labelled as combined because it cannot isolate a cause | Favourable 4 against unfavourable P1, P5, P10 less the Q6 coding, so P5 and P10 (2) | No evidence | No evidence (P4 dropped by row 10, P5 dropped by row 11) | No, but H2 and H3 change from contradicted to untested |

## Reading the table

Row 8, row 12 and row 21 are the most consequential for the favoured reading. They show that the statement "H2 and H3 are contradicted" depends on accepting hypothetical, sometimes hedged or conditional, statements as evidence, and on reading them as evidence about the AI and the moment of disclosure. Under the strictest rules the contradiction disappears and H2 and H3 become untested.

The same rows never produce support. No quote says a participant would stay on the line after learning it is an AI, and none says a participant would decline to ask for a human. The nearest case is P4 in Q5, whose early wish for a human fades, which is a change of mind about a process, not a statement about H3 as worded.

H1 moves between a tie (3 against 3) and 4 against 2 or 4 against 1, depending on how P1 and P4 are coded and on whether context-specific complaints count. It never reaches a clear favourable result on the comparison the hypothesis states, because no quote compares the AI with traditional voice automation directly (rows 0, 17).

Rows 1 to 6 show that no single participant decides the result. The H3 and H2 contradictions each fall to one participant when P4, P5 or P10 is left out, so each depends on two people.

## Does the conclusion reverse?

No row reverses the conclusion. No row produces explicit support for H1 as a comparison, for H2 or for H3, and the overall reading that the interviews do not support the three hypotheses as a set stays the same in all 21 changed rows.

Two parts of the favoured reading are less stable than the rest. The statement that H2 and H3 are contradicted weakens to "untested" under rows 8, 12 and 21, and rests on one participant each under rows 4, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11. The H1 split is a tie or a 4 against 2 lean, depending on rows 2 to 4, 14 and 15. The stable parts are that nothing affirms H2 or H3, that H1 cannot be tested against traditional voice automation, and that the hang-up and human-request statements are tied to the introduction and to the scenario.

## Assumptions and limitations

- Each row changes one rule, except row 21, which is combined and labelled. The rows are not exhaustive. Other defensible rules could be varied, such as weighting by quote length or by how explicit a statement is.
- The tallies use the codings from the eight result files, which were produced by single readers without a second coder. Rows 13 to 18 vary the codings that differ between the files, and other borderline codings (Q4, Q10 on H1) were not varied.
- The material gives no basis for choosing the ten quotes, and P8 and P9 have no quote. Counts are of selected quotes and of six participants. They are not rates, and no row can show how common any view is in the eight interviews or among customers.
- Every H2 and H3 statement is a hypothetical intention after listening to prerecorded scenarios. Row 8 shows the effect of excluding them, and no row can show behaviour in a live call.
- The material does not say whether or when the AI was disclosed, or which scenario each quote refers to apart from the motor claim reference in Q7. Rows 12 and 16 vary the readings but cannot supply these facts.
- Row 20 uses invented positions for P8 and P9 only to bound the result. It is not evidence.
- The technique tests how much the result depends on the choices made. It does not test whether the hypotheses are true.

## Alternative explanations

- The stability of the direction across rows may reflect how the quotes were selected. A selection that included strong reactions on both sides would produce a near-even split under almost any rule, so the robustness would describe the selection and not the interviews.
- Stated intentions about hanging up or asking for a human may follow the situation rather than the AI. P5's reactions are tied to a car accident (Q7), and P10's hang-up is tied to a long introduction (Q8). The result in rows 11, 12 and 16 is consistent with context and introduction design driving the pattern.
- The favourable quotes (Q1 to Q3) may reflect a low baseline from earlier chat bots and robot voices, not greater satisfaction than traditional voice automation. This would leave H1 unsupported even where the direction is favourable.
- Participants who spoke favourably may simply not have been asked about hanging up or requesting a human, so the empty cells for P1, P2 and P3 may reflect the questions or the quote selection and not a view.

specs.CM1-05: The result is a matrix with one row per case and one column per question asked of every case, each cell holding that case's answer. It names the patterns that are consistent across cases and the deviant cases.
specs.TC1-17: The result is a table with one row per changed assumption or inclusion rule and the result obtained under each, alongside the original result. It ends by stating whether the conclusion reverses under any row.
specs.HE1-14: The result is a matrix with one row per case and one column per theme, each cell holding a short summary of the coded data for that case and theme. It notes the empty cells and states what reading across the rows and down the columns shows.
specs.HE1-15: The result is a category structure or a table of category frequencies, with one row per category and a count or interpretation of how often the category is used. It reports agreement between coders where more than one coder was used.
specs.TC1-13: The result lists the hypotheses and gives a matrix of evidence items against hypotheses with a consistency rating in each cell. It names the evidence items that discriminate between hypotheses and the hypothesis with the fewest inconsistencies.
specs.DM-02: The result is a tree in which the main claim is split into the sub-claims that must all be true for it to be true, down to leaf claims. It lists the leaf claims for which no evidence is possible.
specs.HE1-13: The result is a set of themes, each with a name, a description of the pattern of meaning it captures, and data extracts that support it. It ends with a written account that interprets the themes across the data.
specs.MM-10: The result is a table with one row per text and target, giving the stance label of favour, oppose, neutral or none. It reports stance by source and over time, and the share of none labels.
specs.CK-17: The result is a pass or fail list with one row per extracted statement, giving the statement, the exact passage it points to, whether that passage exists by string match and whether the passage supports the claim. It ends with the list of statements that failed.
specs.PE-02: The result has the cleaned text or document-term matrix, a log listing every cleaning rule applied, and a sensitivity table showing the main result under each cleaning regime. It ends by stating whether the themes or rankings changed across regimes.
specs.TC1-16: The result names the claim under test, lists the evidence that would contradict it, and records for each item whether it was found or not found. It states the search used for each item and ends with what the findings mean for the claim.
